card.name: Stiletto dance
card.tagline: A high-performance fusion of jazz, hip-hop, and ballroom executed in stiletto heels.
card.profile: Stiletto dance is a contemporary solo performance genre defined by the use of high-heeled footwear, primarily seen in pop music videos and professional stage productions. It synthesizes technical elements from jazz, ballroom, and hip-hop into a high-energy discipline used by backup dancers and fitness enthusiasts. The style emphasizes fluid arm movements, dynamic footwork, and precise body isolations. Today, it is practiced both as a professional performance art and a specialized fitness movement in dance studios across the United States and Europe.
card.insight: Emerging in the late 20th century, this professional stage style requires dancers to execute complex torso isolations and floor work while balanced on the narrow point of a stiletto heel.

card.profile_long:
Stiletto dance emerged and evolved in the United States and Europe during the late 20th and early 21st centuries as a distinct performance medium. The genre is inextricably linked to the stiletto heel, a shoe style that dictates the dancer's posture and center of gravity. Unlike social dances, stiletto dance is designed for the stage, specifically for the high-production environments of cruise ship entertainment, professional music videos, and backup routines for pop artists. Its development was influenced by the historical 'showgirl' tradition, which was the first technical dance style to incorporate heels into performance choreography.

The movement vocabulary of stiletto dance is a complex hybrid of several established disciplines. It draws its foundational footwork from jazz dance, ballroom, and Latin styles, which provide the necessary structure for navigating the stage in heels. These elements are layered with torso isolations derived from belly dance and hip-hop, creating a contrast between the rigid requirements of the footwear and the fluid movement of the upper body. Additionally, the style incorporates floor work and body language influenced by exotic and contemporary dance, requiring significant core strength and flexibility to execute transitions safely and aesthetically.

In the modern era, stiletto dance has expanded beyond the professional stage into the realm of physical fitness and leisure. It is frequently taught in dance studios and gyms as a specialized movement discipline for women, focusing on empowerment, balance, and coordination. Despite this shift toward fitness, the core techniques remain rooted in professional choreography. The dance is characterized by its adaptability, often appearing in pop and hip-hop music videos where the visual impact of the heels complements the rhythmic intensity of the music. The evolution of the style continues to be driven by the commercial entertainment industry, where it remains a staple of modern choreography.

Technically, the dance requires a mastery of weight distribution. Because the stiletto heel provides a very small surface area for contact with the floor, dancers must maintain a high level of engagement in the ankles and core. The use of 'showgirl' techniques provides the historical basis for this, teaching dancers how to maintain lines and extensions while elevated. The inclusion of go-go dancing styles adds a layer of rhythmic bounce and energy, while the contemporary and exotic dance influences introduce a level of floor-based athleticism that challenges the traditional limitations of high-heeled footwear. This synthesis makes stiletto dance one of the most physically demanding commercial dance forms practiced today.

sections.origins_and_history: The style emerged in the late 20th and early 21st centuries across the United States and Europe. It evolved from the technical foundations of showgirl dance, which was the first style to perform technical choreography in heels, and was later shaped by the demands of the pop music video industry.
sections.how_it_is_danced: It is a solo dance characterized by dynamic footwork and torso isolations. Dancers perform a mix of jazz-based steps, ballroom-influenced movements, and hip-hop isolations. The technique includes significant floor work and fluid arm movements, all executed while wearing stiletto heels.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is typically performed to pop and hip-hop music. The rhythm and tempo are dictated by the commercial tracks used in music videos or stage performances, often featuring strong beats that support sharp isolations and rhythmic footwork.
sections.costume_and_setting: The defining costume element is the stiletto heel shoe. Settings range from professional stages and cruise ships to music video sets and dance studios or gyms for fitness-based practice.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Stiletto dance is primarily a professional performance art used in the entertainment industry. It also serves as a physical fitness discipline for women, focusing on movement vocabulary and body language.
sections.regional_variants: The style is practiced throughout the United States and Europe, though specific regional variations in technique are not detailed in the sources.
sections.lineage: It descends from showgirl dance and incorporates elements from jazz, ballroom, Latin, belly dance, hip-hop, exotic dance, and contemporary dance.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Strong backbeat with electronic or synthesized percussion typical of pop and hip-hop.
music_profile.sound_description: The sound is defined by modern commercial production, featuring heavy basslines and sharp percussive elements that facilitate the 'hits' and isolations in the choreography.

movement_profile.posture: Upright with an engaged core to manage the forward shift in center of gravity caused by heels.
movement_profile.footwork: Dynamic steps based on jazz and ballroom; requires constant awareness of the heel's placement.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Fluid and expressive, drawing from exotic and contemporary dance styles.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Heavy use of isolations borrowed from belly dance and hip-hop.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Solo performance; utilizes both vertical space and floor levels.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Sharp and punctuated during isolations; fluid during transitions.

signature_moves.name: Torso Isolation
signature_moves.description: Independent movement of the chest or hips while the rest of the body remains still.

signature_moves.name: Floor work
signature_moves.description: Athletic movements performed on the ground, transitioning from standing to floor and back.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Frequent level changes from standing to floor; jumps are rare due to heel stability risks.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid locking knees; avoid placing full weight on the heel during rapid lateral movements to prevent ankle injury.

seniors.seated_version: Perform torso and arm isolations while seated in a stable chair; wear flat, supportive shoes instead of heels.
seniors.standing_version: Use a ballet barre or sturdy chair for balance; perform footwork in flat shoes or low, wide heels.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Reduce tempo by 50%; limit the range of torso movements to avoid strain.
seniors.counts: Standard 4/4 counts, focusing on one movement per two beats.

children.game_version: Focus on 'statue' isolations (moving only one body part at a time) to pop music.
